hops.afterHeading: From a flat plate to a tube
hops.title: Tailless Manx cats and the tail-end spinal cord
hops.text: Breeders sort Manx cats into "rumpies," with no tail at all, and "stumpies," with a short stub. In 2013, geneticists found that 95 percent of the short-tailed Manx cats they tested carry a truncating mutation in one copy of the T gene, which makes the protein Brachyury. In mouse embryos, Brachyury is active in the tail bud, the tissue that builds the lowest spinal cord by secondary neurulation. Manx taillessness has long gone with spina bifida, hind-leg problems and incontinence in some kittens. That fits a shared tail-bud origin, though a direct link to the T mutations has not been shown.

sources.citation: Lee et al., Child's Nervous System 38:2101-2111 (2022)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fluffy ginger Manx cat sitting on a coastal stone wall, showing its rounded tailless rump.
image.caption: Most short-tailed Manx cats tested carry a Brachyury mutation, and some tailless kittens have lower-spine defects.

hops.title: Hair patterns on your forearm
hops.text: Look at the hair on your forearm, or at the whorl on the crown of a friend's head. Mammals from mice to humans grow hair in large-scale patterns like these. In mouse skin, global alignment of follicles with the body axes depends on planar cell polarity signaling, the same system required for neural plate convergent extension and neural tube closure. When researchers at Johns Hopkins deleted Frizzled6 in mice, the smooth coat broke into whorls on the hind feet and tufts on the head. Delete Frizzled3 as well, and the mice also end up with an open neural tube.

sources.citation: Wang, Guo & Nathans, Journal of Neuroscience 26:2147-2156 (2006)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student's forearm resting on a wooden desk beside a small brown mouse with a raised tuft of fur on top of its head.
image.caption: In mice, planar cell polarity aligns hair follicles globally with the body axes and helps close the neural tube.

hops.title: Marmite, monkeys, and four tons of spinach
hops.text: The story of folate starts with a jar of yeast spread. In 1930s Bombay, the British pathologist Lucy Wills studied a severe, often fatal anemia of pregnancy among undernourished textile workers. She found that cheap yeast extract from the Marmite company treated the anemia in her hospital patients and in monkeys on a deficient diet. The unknown antianemia activity became known as the "Wills factor," and later work traced it to a form of folate. In 1941, biochemists in Texas concentrated a growth factor from four tons of spinach and named it folic acid, after folium, the Latin word for leaf.

sources.citation: Al-Gailani, Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences 47:229-242 (2014)
Wills, British Medical Journal 1:1059-1064 (1931), reprinted in Nutrition Reviews 36:149-151 (1978)
Mitchell, Snell & Williams, Journal of the American Chemical Society 63:2284 (1941)
Rosenberg, Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism 61:231-235 (2012)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small unlabeled jar of dark yeast spread beside a towering pile of fresh green spinach leaves in wicker baskets on a wooden table.
image.caption: A yeast spread that treated a severe pregnancy anemia gave an early clue to folate; spinach inspired its name.
